shortDef: Models that produce new text, images, audio or code.
longDef: Rather than classifying an input, generative models produce an output that did not exist before, from a prompt or another input. For designers the shift is that outputs are probabilistic: the same request can produce different results, so interfaces need to handle variation, review and correction. Designing the review step is usually more important than designing the input.
example: A summary feature that generates a draft, marks it as generated, and puts it in an editor rather than publishing it.
misuse: Not all AI is generative. Recommendation, search ranking and classification are long-standing uses that produce no new content.

shortDef: A model trained on text that predicts likely continuations.
longDef: LLMs generate plausible text by predicting what follows, which makes them fluent, flexible and unreliable about facts in the same breath. They have a context limit, no inherent access to your data, and no way to know when they are wrong. Every design decision around them follows from those three properties.
example: A feature that answers questions about your documents needs those documents supplied as context; the model does not know them.
misuse: Fluency is not accuracy. Confident phrasing is a property of the model, not evidence that the answer is right.

shortDef: The instruction and context given to a model to produce an output.
longDef: A prompt combines the user's request with instructions, examples and context the product supplies behind the scenes. Much of the design work is deciding what the product adds silently — tone, constraints, format — so the user does not have to. Exposing a blank prompt box puts the burden on the user and produces wildly variable results.
example: A rewrite feature offering "shorter", "plainer" and "more formal" rather than an empty instruction field.
misuse: Prompt engineering is not a substitute for interface design. If the user has to phrase it well, the product has not done its job.

shortDef: A model producing confident output that is simply false.
longDef: Because generation optimises for plausibility, models invent citations, quotes, prices and facts in the same tone as correct ones. There is no reliable internal signal for it, so the interface has to carry the burden: cite sources, show what the answer was drawn from, and make verification cheap. Never present generated content as authoritative without a route to check it.
example: A generated summary attributes a statistic to a real report that does not contain it, phrased exactly like a true citation.
misuse: The word implies a perceptual error. The model is not mistaken about reality; it has no model of reality to be mistaken about.

shortDef: Supplying a model with retrieved documents to answer from.
longDef: Relevant material is looked up first and passed to the model as context, so answers are grounded in specific sources rather than in training data. It reduces invention and, importantly for design, makes citation possible — you can show which passage an answer came from. Retrieval quality then becomes the limiting factor, and a failed retrieval is invisible to the user unless the interface says so.
example: A help assistant that answers from your own documentation and links the paragraph it used.

shortDef: A system that plans and takes actions to reach a goal.
longDef: Agents chain model calls with tools — searching, writing files, calling APIs — to pursue an objective across several steps. The design problems are consent and legibility: what the agent may do without asking, how progress is shown, and how a user stops or reverses it. Irreversible actions taken on a user's behalf need explicit confirmation.
example: An assistant that drafts replies and queues them, requiring one confirmation before anything is sent.

shortDef: Keeping a person's judgement inside an automated process.
longDef: The person reviews, corrects or approves before an output takes effect, which is the main safeguard against confident errors. It only works if review is genuinely possible: enough context, enough time, and no pressure to rubber-stamp. Automation bias is real — people accept a machine's suggestion more readily than a colleague's.
example: Generated alt text presented pre-filled and editable, requiring a deliberate save before it is published.
misuse: A confirmation button is not oversight if the reviewer cannot see what they are approving or is shown fifty an hour.

shortDef: Making it clear why a system produced a particular output.
longDef: Users need enough of the reasoning to decide whether to trust a result: which sources were used, which signals mattered, how confident the system is. Full technical interpretability is rarely available, so interface-level explanation — provenance, confidence and the ability to inspect inputs — carries the weight. In several regulated domains it is a legal requirement.
example: A recommendation labelled "because you saved three accessibility terms", with a control to change that signal.

shortDef: Systematic unfairness in a system's outputs across groups.
longDef: Bias enters through training data that reflects historical inequity, through proxies that stand in for protected characteristics, and through evaluation that only measures the average case. It surfaces as worse performance for accents, skin tones, names or dialects outside the majority. Testing has to be disaggregated by group, because an aggregate accuracy figure hides it completely.
example: Speech input with materially higher error rates for some regional accents, invisible in the overall accuracy number.

shortDef: An interface where the main interaction is exchanging messages.
longDef: Chat is flexible and unusually undiscoverable: a blank field advertises nothing about what the system can do. The strongest designs pair it with visible affordances — suggested prompts, structured results, controls embedded in replies. Chat suits open-ended requests and is a poor replacement for a form or a list.
example: An assistant offering three starting questions and returning a filterable list rather than a paragraph.
misuse: Replacing a working form with a chatbot usually adds turns to a task that took one screen.

shortDef: An interface operated and answered by speech.
longDef: Speech has no visible state and no scrollback, so working memory carries everything and answers must be short. Error recovery is the core design problem: what happens when the system mishears, and how the user corrects it without repeating the whole request. Voice excels hands-free and struggles with anything requiring comparison.
example: "Set a reminder for seven" answered with "Reminder at seven this evening — is that right?" rather than silent action.

shortDef: Using more than one input or output channel together.
longDef: Combining speech, touch, vision and haptics lets people use whichever channel suits the moment, which is both an accessibility gain and a practical one when hands or eyes are busy. Each mode needs to carry enough on its own, since any of them may be unavailable. Handing off mid-task between modes is the hard part.
example: Asking a question aloud and receiving a spoken summary alongside a list on screen that can be scrolled.

shortDef: Changing what someone sees based on what is known about them.
longDef: Personalisation can be explicit, from stated preferences, or implicit, inferred from behaviour. Implicit adaptation risks making the interface unpredictable and unlearnable, and it can feel intrusive when the inference is visibly accurate. Explaining why something is shown, and allowing it to be corrected, is what keeps it acceptable.
example: Surfacing recently viewed terms is welcome; silently reordering the main navigation per user is not.
misuse: Personalisation is not customisation. One is the system deciding; the other is the user deciding.

shortDef: A system that suggests items it predicts you will want.
longDef: Recommendations are generated from similarity between items, between users, or both, and they shape what most people ever see in a large catalogue. Design decisions include how much diversity to keep, how to handle a brand-new user, and whether to explain each suggestion. Optimising purely for immediate clicks tends to narrow what anyone is shown over time.
example: "Related terms" derived from cross-links rather than popularity, so rarely visited entries remain reachable.

shortDef: Interfaces placed in or over three-dimensional space.
longDef: Augmented reality overlays content on the world, virtual reality replaces it, and the umbrella term covers both. Design gains depth, gaze, physical scale and comfort as materials and constraints: content too close causes strain, and unanchored movement causes nausea. Text remains hard, so information density has to fall sharply compared with a screen.
example: Anchoring a label to a real object so it stays put as the viewer moves, rather than floating fixed in view.

shortDef: Computing that works in the background without demanding attention.
longDef: Sensors, wearables and connected devices act on context rather than waiting for explicit commands, so the interface is often a light, a sound or nothing at all. The design principles are restraint and legibility: only interrupt when it matters, and make it possible to find out why something happened. Without that, ambient systems feel like haunted houses.
example: Lights that adjust with the room, with a visible log and an override, rather than changing for reasons nobody can inspect.
